newsitem.title: USA: RESEARCH ALERT - Cowen ups Intel EPS view.
newsitem.headline: RESEARCH ALERT - Cowen ups Intel EPS view.

text.p: -- Cowen & Co analyst Drew Peck said he boosted his earnings outlook for Intel Corp's 1997 year based primarily on the chipmaker's lower-than-expected price cuts on its high volume 133 and 166 megahertz Pentium microprocessors.
-- The analyst said Intel's quarterly price reductions, announced earlier, were far more selective than in past quarters, a move he described as an "opportunistic" bid to maximize short-term profits.
-- He said Intel's decision to cut 133 megahertz Pentium pricing by about 34 percent and 166 megahertz chips by about 27 percent was less than the 40 percent or so he had expected.

-- Peck had expected greater price cuts on these two high volume lines -- which he estimated will account for 70 percent of all Intel microchip revenues this quarter -- to make up for Intel's decision to hold prices constant last quarter.

-- The analyst said he boosted his 1997 estimate to $8.20 per share from $8.10 based on the increased profits he expects the company to generate in the first and second quarters on the 133 and 166 megahertz Pentium lines.

-- He said the benefit of Intel's less-than-expected cuts on these two models was only likely to extend two quarters before rival Advanced Micro Devices Inc introduces competing chips, forcing Intel to make steeper cuts.
-- In the meantime, Peck said Intel is able to exploit its "quasi-monopolistic" market position to skim as much profit as it can from its unique market position.
-- Peck said Intel's decision to maintain pricing on most Pentium Pro models relected the fact that demand for these high-powered chips is not particularly price sensitive.

-- He noted that the company is expected to introduce a more powerful line of Pentium Pro chips code-named Klamath in the second quarter which may require the company to cut prices on existing Pentium Pro models at that time.

-- The analyst contrasted the selective price-cutting plan for the first quarter to the broad-stroke reductions seen in prior periods. "Historically, (Intel) tended to take a broad (percentage) slice off the whole line," he said.
